fields.content: Within 90 days, several teams pilot graph-centered agent workflows in narrow maintenance lanes such as dependency bumps, flaky test repair, and documentation sync, but rollout stalls at the boundary where graph updates imply cross-repository architectural changes. The failure mode is not raw model quality; it is missing fitness functions for system-level coherence. Local success metrics (tests green, lint clean, ticket closed) reward edits that slowly increase coupling and hidden operational risk. The dominant narrative says typed artifact graphs solve coordination, but in practice the graph is only as trustworthy as the freshness of its edges, and most orgs still lack automated provenance for docs, runbooks, tickets, and infra state.
fields.counterfactual: If teams mistake local graph completeness for genuine system understanding, they will expand autonomy before they can detect architectural drift, leading to a visible rollback from agent-driven change programs.

fields.content: Economics of disappointment emerge as teams discover that directed software evolution requires expensive surrounding structure: graph extraction, artifact normalization, eval maintenance, and human review bandwidth. In the next 90 days, CFO and engineering leadership scrutiny shifts from “can the agent edit code?” to “what is the fully loaded cost per safe merged change?” Vendors that price on seat expansion or raw token consumption face pushback because savings are eroded by verification overhead and integration work. The likely near-term winner is not the most autonomous system but the one that reduces toil in preexisting workflows without demanding a full graph-native operating model.
fields.counterfactual: If buyers continue assuming autonomy automatically lowers cost, they will overcommit to platform rewrites and then retrench sharply when measured ROI fails to appear within one budget cycle.

The field is not yet ready for “self-evolving” claims at organization scale because graph semantics, tool availability, and model stochasticity still vary across runs. fields.counterfactual: If vendors keep selling full self-evolution before reproducibility and accountability improve, the backlash will not just slow adoption of autonomous coding; it will also taint adjacent graph-based engineering approaches that could have succeeded under narrower claims.

fields.content: Within 90 days, the strongest selection pressure shifts from raw code-generation throughput to survivability inside governance-constrained delivery systems. Teams piloting directed software evolution wire mutation loops to CI, policy checks, and rollback gates, but the winning pattern is not the most autonomous agent. It is the lineage-aware workflow that can explain why a change was proposed, what fitness function it optimized, and how it can be reversed. This mirrors regulated biological systems: traits spread when they improve reproductive success under environmental constraints, not when they maximize local metabolic speed. Concretely, platform teams at larger enterprises and infrastructure-heavy startups start requiring provenance graphs, eval traces, and bounded blast-radius policies before agent-written changes can merge.
fields.counterfactual: If the field continues optimizing only for coding speed, early failures in compliance, rollback, and incident analysis will make autonomous evolution look reckless and slow enterprise adoption.

fields.content: Within 90 days, practitioner adoption concentrates on agent-assisted maintenance workflows rather than full self-evolving product systems. The most credible near-term pattern is a graph-backed change loop that links tickets, code spans, tests, CI results, and deployment metadata, then lets an agent propose bounded patches behind existing pull-request review. The visible signal is vendors and internal platform teams shipping issue-to-PR pipelines with artifact lineage and automatic rollback hooks instead of promising end-to-end autonomous product delivery.
fields.counterfactual: If teams ignore this bounded-adoption pattern and design only for full autonomy, they will miss the segment where real production trust is won: repetitive maintenance work with strong test and policy scaffolding.

fields.counterfactual: If vendors continue optimizing for breadth of autonomous claims instead of narrow operational reliability, buyers will increasingly bypass them for simpler workflow tools that offer clearer accountability and lower failure blast radius.

fields.content: From an organizational-theory lens, directed software evolution is entering a bureaucratization phase: policy gates, replay logs, approval hooks, and provenance standards become the equivalent of internal accounting controls. This raises legitimacy and adoption in large enterprises, but it also shifts competitive advantage toward teams that can minimize coordination overhead per approved change rather than teams that merely maximize raw patch generation.
fields.counterfactual: If teams treat governance only as a compliance tax, they will underestimate how approval latency and review handoffs become the real throughput bottleneck, causing agent programs to stall despite strong model output quality.

fields.content: Biology offers a useful warning: increasing mutation rate without correspondingly strong selection functions produces noisy local adaptation, not robust evolution. In software terms, more agent-generated patches, refactors, and workflow steps will create surface-level velocity, but without durable fitness signals for architecture, incident rate, operator burden, and long-range maintainability, systems drift toward brittle complexity masked by short-term success metrics.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations ignore the need for better selection mechanisms, they may mistake rapid change volume for system improvement and only discover accumulated degradation during outages, migrations, or audit events.

fields.counterfactual: If platform teams assume the graph is self-maintaining, recommendation quality will deteriorate, users will route around the system, and the control plane may be dismissed as another stale enterprise metadata layer.

fields.content: By day 30-60, teams building Directed Software Evolution systems will converge on policy-enforced execution loops rather than fully autonomous free-running agents: planners will propose changes, evaluators will score them, and guarded executors will apply only bounded patches behind approval or test gates. The near-term adoption path is orchestrators that combine repo state, benchmark suites, and explicit policy checks, not open-ended self-modification.
fields.counterfactual: If builders ignore this and ship unconstrained self-editing agents, reliability incidents and rollback costs will dominate, causing enterprises to freeze pilots and push the category back toward human-only review workflows.

fields.content: The most technically feasible early wedge is repository-scoped evolutionary improvement on measurable objectives such as test pass rate, latency, cloud cost, alert reduction, and policy compliance. Systems that can generate many small candidate patches, evaluate them in CI sandboxes, and preserve a searchable lineage of accepted versus rejected mutations will outperform single-shot coding agents.
fields.counterfactual: If teams fail to instrument objective functions and lineage, they will not know whether evolution is improving the system or merely producing noisy code churn, and the field will plateau at impressive demos without compounding gains.

fields.content: A practical bottleneck will be evaluation infrastructure, not raw model intelligence. Organizations will discover that stable replay environments, seeded workloads, deterministic integration tests, and policy engines like Cedar or OPA are prerequisites for safe software evolution. fields.counterfactual: If the field keeps overemphasizing smarter frontier models without investing in evaluation and governance infrastructure, production deployments will remain narrow because every change will still require expensive human trust reconstruction.

fields.content: From economics, the field starts to resemble a market with high transaction costs: every agentic change carries verification, coordination, and governance overhead. The result is a Coase-like boundary shift where firms internalize agent infrastructure into shared platform layers rather than letting each product team run bespoke autonomous loops. Expect central policy services, shared eval datasets, and budget controls to expand faster than fully self-directing product agents.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations underestimate transaction costs, they proliferate local agent stacks, duplicate evaluation work, and lose the savings that justified directed evolution in the first place.
